name: Jummah Masjid
address: Royal Road, Queen St, Port Louis, Mauritius
description: Port Louis's principal mosque, on Royal Road in the heart of the old commercial quarter. Members of the city's mercantile community bought the site on Queen Street in 1852 and consecrated the mosque in 1853, when it was known as the "Mosque of the Arabs." A major expansion begun in 1878, overseen by Jackaria Jan Mahomed, was delayed for years by disease and construction-supply shortages and wasn't finished until 1895 - the building seen today is largely that late-19th-century enlargement.
interesting_fact: The mosque blends Indian, Creole and Islamic architectural styles, and is widely described as one of the most beautiful religious buildings in Mauritius. A marble tomb beside the mosque holds the remains of Jamal Shah, a pir (Sufi holy man) from Kutch in India.

name: Government House
description: The seat of Mauritius's colonial and now national government, at the top of Place d'Armes. The first Government House, built of wood in 1725 under the French, was destroyed by a cyclone in 1727. Construction of a permanent building began under French governors Nicolas de Maupin and Mahé de Labourdonnais, who enlarged it into the building's current footprint in 1738, originally named the Hôtel du Gouvernement.
interesting_fact: Place d'Armes, the grand palm-lined boulevard leading up to it, is often called the most iconic street in Mauritius and is lined with statues of figures from the island's history.
source_notes: GPS: Google Places, chosen from 3 candidates (also matched "Government House Police Post", "Sterling House" - address and location both point clearly to the main building). History from Lonely Planet/Holidify via WebSearch.

name: Place d'Armes
description: The grand royal-palm-lined boulevard running from Government House down to the waterfront, and the most iconic public space in Port Louis. Originally the site of a fortification and battery built by Governor De Nyon and later reinforced by Mahe de Labourdonnais, it was laid out as the ceremonial approach to Government House, the French colonial residence dating to 1738. Today the avenue is lined with statues of the figures who shaped the island's history, from colonial governors like Sir William Stevenson and Sir John Pope Hennessy to Queen Victoria and lawyer Sir William Newton, who helped democratise Mauritius's electoral system.
interesting_fact: At the quayside end of the avenue stands a bronze statue of Mahe de Labourdonnais, cast by French sculptor A. Dumont and inaugurated on 30 August 1859 - it has since become one of the most recognised emblems of Port Louis itself.

name: Central Market Port Louis
description: The historic heart of Port Louis's daily life, dating to 1839 under British colonial rule (the market itself traces back further, to a 1828 origin before moving to this site in 1833). Its wrought-iron gates, decorated with floral motifs and dating from 1839, are a well-known piece of the city's Victorian-era heritage. The building was heavily renovated between 2001 and 2004 after several fires, while its original character was preserved.
interesting_fact: For nearly two centuries the market has been a meeting point for all of Mauritius's communities - Creole, Franco-Mauritian, Indian, Chinese and African - trading side by side, and it's still often called the Bazaar or Victoria Market by locals.

name: Champ de Mars
description: Home to the Champ de Mars Racecourse, inaugurated on 25 June 1812 by the Mauritius Turf Club - the oldest horse-racing club in the Southern Hemisphere and the second-oldest in the world. Before it was a racecourse, French governor Mahé de La Bourdonnais used the ground as a military training field for his troops.
interesting_fact: When Mauritius became independent on 12 March 1968, the flag-hoisting ceremony marking the occasion was held here at the Champ de Mars - tying the island's oldest sporting institution to its newest chapter as a nation.

name: Citadelle (Fort Adelaide)
description: Also known as Fort Adelaide, this hilltop citadel overlooking Port Louis was built by the British between 1830 and 1840, named after Queen Adelaide, consort of King William IV. It was built to guard against invasion and control local unrest amid racial tensions of the period, using hundreds of Indian contractors over six years of construction.
interesting_fact: Despite its imposing basalt-stone walls, the fort was never actually used in combat, and today survives as the best-preserved of the major British fortresses built on the island.

name: Cannon Stand
address: 69 Emmanuel Anquetil St, Port Louis, Mauritius
description: A row of cast-iron cannons mounted on wooden carriages along the ramparts of the Citadelle (Fort Adelaide), still aimed out over Port Louis harbour just as they were when the fort was completed. Built from black basalt in a Moorish style between 1830 and 1840 under British colonial rule, the fort was raised to guard against a feared French invasion and to help control local opposition to the abolition of slavery, though its guns were, in the end, never fired in anger.
interesting_fact: Despite bristling with cannons and room for a 200-strong garrison, Fort Adelaide never saw combat - it functioned instead as a show of force overlooking the harbour, and today its ramparts are better known as one of the best viewpoints over Port Louis and the surrounding mountains.

name: Blue Penny Museum
description: A museum dedicated to the history and art of Mauritius, at Caudan Waterfront, opened in November 2001. Its centrepiece is the pair of 1847 "Post Office" stamps - the one-penny orange-red and two-pence blue - among the rarest and most valuable stamps in the world, whose designs were based on Britain's Penny Black and feature Queen Victoria's profile.
interesting_fact: A consortium of Mauritian companies, led by the Mauritius Commercial Bank, paid $2,000,000 in 1993 to buy the stamps back to the island after almost 150 years abroad. To protect them from light damage, the originals are only illuminated for ten minutes on the quarter-past of every opening hour - the rest of the time, visitors see facsimiles.

name: Aapravasi Ghat World Heritage Site
description: A UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2006, and the place where the modern indentured-labour diaspora began. Built in 1849, the Aapravasi Ghat ("Immigration Depot") was the main entry point for almost 500,000 indentured labourers - mostly from India, but also China, Africa, Madagascar and Southeast Asia - brought to Mauritius between 1849 and 1923, mainly to work the island's sugar plantations after the abolition of slavery.
interesting_fact: Roughly 70% of Mauritians today are descended from these indentured labourers - making this small 1,640 m² depot one of the most significant sites anywhere for understanding the origins of modern Mauritian society, and one of the earliest examples of the labour-migration system that would go on to reshape economies worldwide.

name: Sir Sewoosagur Ramgoolam Statue
description: A statue at Caudan Waterfront of Sir Seewoosagur Ramgoolam, the first Prime Minister of independent Mauritius. Born in 1900 at Belle Rive to an indentured labourer from India, he rose from a self-enrolled mission-school pupil to co-found the Mauritius Labour Party in 1936, campaigning for voting and workers' rights. He served as Mayor of Port Louis, Chief Minister and Premier before leading Mauritius to independence on 12 March 1968 as its first Prime Minister, later serving as Governor-General - a journey still celebrated as the model of the nation's founding story.
interesting_fact: As the first head of the independent government, Ramgoolam established free education, free healthcare and a national social security system - a legacy still commemorated with wreath-laying ceremonies held at statues like this one, and remembered every year on his birthday, 12 September, celebrated as SSR's birth anniversary.

name: Port Louis Fire Station
description: The Port Louis Fire and Rescue Service's main station, a working municipal building housed in a handsome colonial-era structure dating to 1906 - the oldest fire station still in operation in Mauritius. It replaced an earlier station relocated from the port area in 1850, part of the city's long, hard-won response to the devastating fires of 1816 and 1892 that tore through Port Louis when most buildings were still made of wood and straw.
interesting_fact: The station's watch tower once served as a lookout for spotting fires across the city before modern communications existed, and it still houses one of only three surviving Merryweather clocks in the world - a rare mechanical relic from the early era of organised firefighting.

name: Port Louis Theatre
address: Remy Ollier St & Jules Koenig St, Port Louis, Mauritius
description: The Port Louis Theatre, the oldest theatre in the Indian Ocean region. Governor Robert Farquhar laid its first stone in 1820, and architect Pierre Poujade built it in the style of classic London playhouses, with the theatre inaugurated on 11 June 1822. Inside, three tiers of seating for around 600 sit beneath an ornately painted dome ceiling of cherubs and chandeliers, and for over a century it was the island's sole home for opera, drama and balls, until the Plaza Theatre opened in Rose Hill in 1933.
interesting_fact: The idea of bringing theatre to Mauritius dates back even earlier than the building itself - a French warship's health officer first brought a troupe to perform in Port Louis in 1790, though it was disbanded just two years later by a smallpox epidemic.

name: Aurelie Perrine Passenger Terminal
description: A passenger ferry terminal on the Port Louis waterfront, run by the Mauritius Ports Authority and operated by Mauritius Shipping Corporation under the Coraline service. description: A historic public cemetery at the eastern edge of Port Louis, in the Roche Bois neighbourhood close to the docks, entered through a dark basalt archway topped with a cross. name: Fort George
description: The site of Fort George, the largest stone fortification ever built in Mauritius, guarding the northern entrance to Port Louis harbour. A fortification has stood on this ground since Mahe de Labourdonnais's time in 1730, but the British rebuilt it in earnest in the 19th century - named for King George III and IV - both to deter a French attack and to keep the island's slave-owning planters in check after the 1831 Mauritius Rebellion. By 1882 it carried a mix of upgraded Rifled Muzzle Loading guns, making it the most heavily armed post at the harbour mouth.
interesting_fact: Fort George was declared a national monument in 1998 and reconfirmed as national heritage in 2003, but much of the site has fallen into serious disrepair - heritage campaigners have pushed for years to save what remains of Mauritius's largest stone fort from being lost for good.

name: Christian Decotter Cruise Terminal
description: A cruise-ship passenger terminal on the Port Louis waterfront at Les Salines, named after Christian Decotter, a Mauritian aviation and tourism figure who spent decades in commercial aviation and travel management with companies including Rogers and MTTB, and headed the Concorde travel agency from 1979. Renovated and reopened in 2008, the terminal was the first in the region able to berth the world's largest cruise ships, cementing Port Louis Harbour's role as the premier cruise hub of the Indian Ocean - a 7,500-square-metre facility able to process up to 4,000 passengers at peak times across two access bridges.
interesting_fact: Decotter became the public face of Mauritian tourism policy in the 1990s: spokesperson for the PMSD party, then appointed Chairman of the Tourism Advisory Board in March 1995 under Minister Xavier-Luc Duval. Off duty he was a keen sportsman - a competitive volleyball and basketball player and multiple island tennis-tournament winner - before his death in July 2003.

name: Pere Laval Church & Museum
address: 27 Ste Croix Rd, Port Louis, Mauritius
description: A major Catholic pilgrimage shrine in the Sainte-Croix district, built around the tomb of Father Jacques-Desire Laval - a French missionary priest and trained doctor who spent nearly 23 years ministering to Mauritius's recently freed slaves and is credited with converting 67,000 people to Christianity. Known as the 'Apostle of Mauritius', he died on 9 September 1864, and more than thirty thousand mourners followed his casket to the tomb opposite the church where it still lies today. He was beatified by Pope John Paul II in 1979, and the site is often described as the Lourdes of the Indian Ocean, with numerous miracles attributed to pilgrims who have visited.
interesting_fact: Every 8 September, people set out from across Mauritius on foot for an overnight march to reach the shrine by his feast day on the 9th - tens of thousands of pilgrims of every faith, some travelling from as far as France, South Africa and Britain, gather to mark the anniversary of his death.

name: Plateau
description: A scenic elevated vantage point ('Le Plateau') above Port Louis, off Military Road, looking out over the packed rooftops of the capital down to the harbour and Indian Ocean beyond. The name reflects the area's role in the city's history: after repeated disasters in Port Louis itself - the great fire of 1816, recurring malaria outbreaks and cyclones - much of the population moved up to this cooler, healthier central plateau, and many residents still live on these slopes today.
interesting_fact: On a clear day the view stretches from the high-rise towers of the city centre, past the harbour's cranes and cargo ships, all the way out to the open ocean - a single sightline over more than two centuries of Port Louis's growth from a fire-prone colonial port to a modern capital.

name: Martello Tower
description: A squat coastal defence tower built by the British between 1832 and 1835, one of five raised around Mauritius after the 1810 conquest from France amid fears of a French counter-attack. Its design copied the Torra di Mortella in Corsica, which had impressed British forces for its thick basalt walls, flat gun roof and self-contained garrison quarters. Restored in 1992 with funding from the Mauritian government and several foreign missions, it reopened as a museum in 2000 and is now a protected national heritage site.
interesting_fact: Despite being purpose-built for war, none of Mauritius's Martello towers ever fired a shot in anger - they were rendered obsolete by advances in artillery before any French attack materialised.

name: Jardins de la Compagnie (Company Garden)
description: Port Louis's oldest and largest public garden, laid out in the 18th century on land first used as a vegetable plot by the French East India Company. Under threat of a smallpox epidemic the ground was pressed into service as a cemetery until the burial ground was moved to the West Cemetery in 1771, after which the site was replanted as an ornamental park. Today its avenues of towering banyan and royal palm trees, fountains and quiet benches make it a favourite lunchtime retreat for office workers in the surrounding capital, and it doubles as an open-air gallery of Mauritian history, dotted with more than a dozen statues and busts of the writers, doctors and independence-era figures who shaped the island.
interesting_fact: Look closely among the trees and you'll find a cluster of individual monuments worth tracking down in their own right, including tributes to journalist Remy Ollier, poet Leoville L'Homme, physiologist Brown-Sequard and civil-rights lawyer Manilal Doctor - each with its own story told elsewhere on this tour.

name: Statue of Remy Ollier

description: A monument in the Company Garden to Remy Ollier (1816-1845), a mixed-race Mauritian journalist often called the father of the island's free press. Barred by his ancestry from full civil rights under colonial rule, Ollier founded the newspaper La Sentinelle de Maurice in 1843 specifically to campaign against the discriminatory laws that denied "free coloured" Mauritians equal status with white colonists, and his agitation helped force reforms within just a few years of the paper's launch.
interesting_fact: Ollier died of tuberculosis in 1845 aged only 28, having spent barely two years as a public campaigner - this monument, unveiled for the centenary of his birth on 15 October 1916, was raised because that brief career was seen as having changed the course of Mauritian civil rights.
